issues.message: This plan files jointly, and a death falls inside its horizon. The year of the death is still filed jointly; from the following year the survivor is taxed as SINGLE -- single brackets, the single standard deduction and single phaseout thresholds, and its Medicare premium, which reads the return from two years before, uses that return's own filing status (joint for the two years after the death, then single) -- and the person who died no longer counts toward the age-65 amounts. QUALIFYING SURVIVING SPOUSE STATUS IS NOT MODELLED: it would keep the joint brackets and the joint standard deduction for the two years after the death, but it requires a dependent child and this plan has no input for one. A household with a dependent child therefore sees a tax in those two years that is TOO HIGH. Head of household and remarriage are not modelled either. The Roth IRA income limit follows the same transition. The HSA family contribution limit is a question of health coverage, not of filing status; the plan has no coverage input, so it keeps the limit the entered status implies, which may overstate a survivor's room.

notModelled: the HSA family limit after the death

issues.message: Part of a traditional IRA contribution in this plan was not deductible, so it becomes basis and is not taxed again when it is distributed. Only basis this projection itself created is counted: nondeductible contributions made before this plan starts, and nontaxable amounts rolled in, are not known to it. A household that already holds an opening basis will see a HIGHER tax here than it would owe.

A spouse dies inside this plan's horizon and the other survives. The survivor is assumed to take the accounts as their OWN from the year after the death (the traditional IRAs from 59 1/2; below): any required distribution from them is figured on the survivor's age and start age, and any nondeductible IRA basis passes with them. In the year of the death itself, a distribution the owner had not yet taken is still due on the owner's own schedule. The survivor is under 59 1/2 at the death, so the deceased's traditional IRAs are held as an inherited IRA, the survivor its sole beneficiary: no 10% additional tax on what is drawn from them (IRC 72(t)(2)(A)(ii)); a required distribution on the survivor's single life expectancy, recalculated each year -- from the year the deceased would have reached their required age where the death came before it, and otherwise from the year after the death on the longer of the two lives (26 CFR 1.401(a)(9)-3(d), -5(d)); and the deceased's nondeductible basis kept in its own pool. The survivor is modelled as treating them as their own from the first year that opens at 59 1/2 or later, or from the year after a contribution is made to them; from then on the survivor's own rules apply. A workplace plan passes as the survivor's own, as before. A taxable account's cost basis resets to its value when it passes, up or down (IRC 1014(a)); the value is read at the opening of the first year after the death, not on the date of death.

issues.message: A spouse dies inside this plan's horizon and the other survives. The survivor is assumed to take the accounts as their OWN from the year after the death: any required distribution from them is figured on the survivor's age and start age, and any nondeductible IRA basis passes with them. In the year of the death itself, a distribution the owner had not yet taken is still due on the owner's own schedule. A survivor under 59 1/2 at the death keeps the deceased's traditional IRAs as an inherited IRA until 59 1/2, without the 10% additional tax (IRC 72(t)(2)(A)(ii)); no traditional IRA passed to a survivor under 59 1/2 here. A taxable account's cost basis resets to its value when it passes, up or down (IRC 1014(a)); the value is read at the opening of the first year after the death, not on the date of death. The plan says the household's property is community property (A.R.S. 25-211(A)), so at the first death the whole cost basis of a joint account, and of the survivor's own taxable accounts, resets to its value (IRC 1014(b)(6)), as the decedent's does. An account titled as joint tenants with right of survivorship rather than as community property (A.R.S. 33-431) may not qualify.
